description: Uzay, teknoloji ve bilime ilgi duyan, farklı becerilerimizi bir araya getirerek yaratıcı projeler geliştirmek isteyen bir ekibiz. Yazılım, yapay zekâ, backend ve veri alanlarıyla ilgileniyoruz. NASA Space Apps Challenge'da birlikte öğrenmek, üretmek ve NASA verilerini kullanarak gerçek bir probleme çözüm geliştirmek istiyoruz.
summary:
LUNA Navigator is an interactive tool that answers two questions: where to land at the lunar south pole, and when.

The south pole promises water ice, but conditions change daily: the same site can move from sunlight and Earth contact to darkness within weeks. Existing rankings freeze regions at one date; LUNA Navigator adds the missing dimension: time.

It evaluates NASA's nine candidate regions against four coupled constraints: terrain slope, solar illumination, direct-to-Earth communications, and proximity to permanently shadowed regions. Slope comes from real NASA LRO LOLA data (80 m and 20 m); 360° horizon ray-casting with lunar curvature correction maps horizon obstruction; and NAIF SPICE ephemerides (de440) give precise Sun and Earth positions. All metrics are scored over NASA's official 6.5-day surface mission window — the same criterion used to select these regions.

Drag the date slider: the ranking changes live. Every region gets a transparent verdict — SUITABLE, CONDITIONAL, or RISKY. KODI, the built-in mission assistant, tours first-time visitors and answers questions from live data.

Built with vanilla JavaScript and a Python pipeline, it is open source, reproducible from NASA data, and live on GitHub Pages.

Team kodeX — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Sivas.
details:
What it does and how it works LUNA Navigator is an interactive decision-support tool that compares NASA's nine candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole — not only by location, but by date. The user picks a mission date; the tool re-scores every region for NASA's official 6.5-day surface window and re-ranks them live, because at the south pole the same site can move from sunlight and Earth contact to darkness within weeks.

Each region is evaluated against four coupled constraints. Terrain slope is computed from real NASA LRO LOLA elevation rasters (80 m resolution, 20 m in key areas) and cross-checked against official LOLA slope records. Solar illumination and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communications come from 360-degree horizon ray-casting — with a lunar-curvature correction term — combined with topocentric Sun and Earth positions from NASA's NAIF SPICE ephemerides (de440). The fourth constraint, proximity to permanently shadowed regions, captures scientific value: safe, sunlit zones within reach of water-ice reservoirs. Every region receives a transparent verdict — SUITABLE, CONDITIONAL, or RISKY — with its reasoning visible on screen.

KODI, a built-in mission assistant, greets first-time visitors with a guided tour of the interface and answers mission questions from the live on-screen data. It runs in two modes: a language-model backend when the server is reachable, and a fully offline rule-based mode otherwise — the interface never breaks.

Benefits and intended impact Landing-site studies typically freeze candidates at a single date. LUNA Navigator makes the calendar a first-class variable and turns NASA-grade analysis into something anyone can explore in a browser: mission planners get a fast pre-screening layer, while students and the public get an accessible window into real Artemis planning trade-offs. The entire pipeline is open source and reproducible from NASA PDS data.

Tools, languages and software Frontend: vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript with a hand-built SVG polar map (no frameworks), hosted on GitHub Pages. Backend pipeline: Python with rasterio, pyproj, NumPy and SciPy for terrain and horizon computation; SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE) for ephemerides; FastAPI for the KODI service. The assistant's online mode uses an open-weight LLM served via the Groq API. AI-generated visuals (background nebula, mascot) are watermarked and declared in our submission form. Development ran entirely on standard laptops — no special hardware.

Creativity The core creative leap is the question itself: "where to land?" became "where — and when?". Around it we built an original combination: a time-scrubbable polar map with a day/night sweep, a verdict system readable at a glance, and a bilingual (TR/EN) assistant that both teaches the tool and explains its own answers.

Factors we considered Lander safety (slope thresholds at 5 and 10 degrees), power generation (illumination across the full mission window), continuous telemetry (DTE line-of-sight against the local horizon), scientific return (PSR proximity), data authenticity (NASA sources only: LOLA and NAIF SPICE), reproducibility (every figure regenerable from raw PDS files), and accessibility (responsive layout, text-labeled verdicts for color-blind users, bilingual interface).
